Queen
KWēN
n. (rendering Hebrew malkâh, g'bīrâh, shēgal, and Greek basilissa)
From Old English cwēn, which meant simply woman or wife — cognate with Greek gunē, woman, and with Gothic qēns. The word rose in dignity over centuries from woman to king's wife to reigning sovereign. Hebrew keeps distinctions English lost: malkâh is a reigning queen or a foreign queen, shēgal is the royal consort, and g'bīrâh is the queen mother — an office of real standing in Judah, since the mother of the reigning king is named in the formula for nearly every reign.

Biblical Definition

Scripture's queens fall into sharply distinguished classes. There is the queen raised up for the deliverance of God's people: Ahasuerus “set the royal crown upon her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti” (Est 2:17), and Mordecai's question — who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this? — states the doctrine of providence that governs the whole book, in which God is never named and never absent. There is the queen who comes seeking wisdom: “when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to prove him with hard questions” (1Ki 10:1) — and the Lord Jesus made her a witness against His own generation, for she came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and a greater than Solomon is here. There is the honoured consort of the royal wedding psalm: “upon thy right hand did stand the queen in gold of Ophir” (Psa 45:9), a psalm the New Testament applies to Christ and which the church has long read of Him and His bride. And there is the counterfeit: the “queen of heaven” to whom the women of Judah burned incense and poured out drink offerings (Jer 44:17), defending the practice to Jeremiah's face on the ground that it had once brought them plenty. Scripture also gives Jezebel and Athaliah, queens who ruled and destroyed, so that the office is honoured or condemned by the character and worship of the woman who holds it.

Webster 1828 Definition

The wife of a king, or a woman who reigns; in Scripture Esther raised up for a providential deliverance, the queen of Sheba who came seeking wisdom and became a witness against unbelief, the honoured consort of the royal psalm, and the false queen of heaven whose worship Jeremiah rebuked.

expand to see more

QUEEN, n. 1. The consort of a king; a queen consort.

2. A woman who is the sovereign of a kingdom; a queen regent; as Elizabeth, queen of England; the queen of Sheba.

3. The word is the Saxon cwen, a woman or wife, answering to the Greek gune; it has risen in dignity from its original sense.

4. Queen mother; the mother of the reigning prince, an office of dignity in the kingdom of Judah, whose name is recorded with each king's reign.

5. Queen of heaven; the title of the idol worshipped by the apostate women of Judah, to whom they burnt incense and poured out drink offerings. Jer. 7; Jer. 44.

Key Scripture

Esther 2:17 — "And the king loved Esther above all the women, and she obtained grace and favour in his sight more than all the virgins; so that he set the royal crown upon her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti."

1 Kings 10:1 — "And when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to prove him with hard questions."

Psalm 45:9 — "Kings' daughters were among thy honourable women: upon thy right hand did stand the queen in gold of Ophir."

Jeremiah 44:17 — "But we will certainly do whatsoever thing goeth forth out of our own mouth, to burn incense unto the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto her, as we have done, we, and our fathers, our kings, and our princes, in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem: for then had we plenty of victuals, and were well, and saw no evil."

Modern Corruption

The title queen of heaven, which Jeremiah records as the name of an idol under judgment, was later applied to the mother of our Lord — a devotion Scripture never authorises and which Jer 44 expressly rebukes.

expand to see more

Jer 44 is one of the most direct confrontations in the prophets, and its subject is precisely this title. The women of Judah in Egypt told Jeremiah they would go on burning incense to the queen of heaven, and their argument is worth noting because it is still used: things went better for us when we did it. The prophet's answer is that the LORD remembered that incense, and that it was the cause of the desolation they were living in. The later application of the same title to the Virgin Mary, together with the doctrines of her immaculate conception, bodily assumption, and mediation, has no warrant in Scripture. Mary is blessed among women, as she herself says all generations shall call her — and her own recorded words point away from herself: whatsoever he saith unto you, do it. To honour her as the faithful mother of our Lord is right; to invoke her, crown her, or make her a mediatrix is to give to a creature what belongs to God alone, for there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.

A second and quite different corruption attaches to Esther, whose book is sometimes dismissed as secular because God is not named in it, or else moralised into a story about a brave young woman being true to herself. Both readings miss the machinery. The book is an extended demonstration of providence working through ordinary means and remarkable coincidences — a sleepless king, a chronicle read at midnight, a gallows built fifty cubits high by the man who would hang on it. Esther's courage is real and is presented as costly, and it rests on Mordecai's assurance that deliverance would arise from another place if she failed. That is not self-actualisation; it is the confidence that God's purpose does not depend on the obedience He nevertheless requires.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew distinguishes malkâh, a reigning or foreign queen; shēgal, the royal consort; and g'bīrâh, the queen mother, a formal office in Judah. Greek basilissa is the feminine of basileus, king.

expand to see more

Hebrew malkâh (H4436) — queen; the word used of Esther, of Vashti, and of the queen of Sheba, feminine of melek, king.

Hebrew g'bīrâh (H1377) — a mistress, a queen mother; from gābar, to be strong. Asa removed Maachah from being g'bīrâh because she had made an idol (1Ki 15:13).

Hebrew shēgal (H7694) — a royal consort; the word rendered queen in Psa 45:9, standing at the king's right hand in gold of Ophir.

Hebrew m'leketh hashshāmayim — queen of heaven; the title of the Assyro-Babylonian goddess Ishtar, worshipped by apostate Judah (Jer 7:18; 44:17).

Greek basilissa (G938) — queen; used of the queen of the south (Mat 12:42), of Candace queen of the Ethiopians (Act 8:27), and of Babylon's boast, I sit a queen (Rev 18:7).

Usage

"Of providential elevation: made her queen instead of Vashti (Est 2:17); for such a time as this (Est 4:14)."

"Of the seeker after wisdom: the queen of Sheba came to prove him with hard questions (1Ki 10:1); the queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment (Mat 12:42)."

"Of false worship and of judgment: the queen of heaven (Jer 44:17); I sit a queen, and am no widow (Rev 18:7)."
